rationale: The Old English verb 'a-nýdan' means to compel or force someone to do something (often against their will), as indicated by the prefix 'a-' (perfective) and the root 'nýdan' (to compel, constrain). This aligns best with drive.v.07 ("compel somebody to do something, often against his own will or judgment"), capturing the coercive sense of the word rather than physical locomotion or herding.
